questions.q: State the agriculture sector growth rate during 1980-91 and 1992-2001 as per Table 3.1 in the NCERT textbook.
questions.a: Agriculture growth was 3.6% during 1980-91 and declined to 3.3% during 1992-2001. A wrong answer (e.g., stating growth increased) reveals the student has not read Table 3.1 carefully or confuses agriculture with services sector growth (which rose from 6.7% to 8.2%). This indicates a failure to distinguish sectoral performance within aggregate GDP growth.

questions.q: Explain why the partial removal of fertiliser subsidy disproportionately affected small and marginal farmers compared to large farmers.
questions.a: Small and marginal farmers operate on thinner margins and have limited access to credit, so a 10-15% rise in fertiliser cost (due to subsidy cut) represents a larger share of their total cultivation cost. Large farmers can absorb the increase through economies of scale and better market access. A wrong answer focusing only on "higher costs for all" misses the distributional impact — the core equity concern in reform assessment.

questions.q: Using the Mahadeva case study: if fertiliser cost rose by ₹2,000 per half-acre due to subsidy removal, and imported edible oil reduced groundnut price by ₹1,000 per quintal (from ₹7,000 to ₹6,000), calculate the new profit/loss per half-acre assuming output remains 2 quintals.
questions.a: Step 1: Original revenue = 2 quintals × ₹7,000 = ₹14,000. Step 2: Original cost = ₹10,000. Step 3: New cost = ₹10,000 + ₹2,000 = ₹12,000. Step 4: New revenue = 2 quintals × ₹6,000 = ₹12,000. Step 5: New profit = ₹12,000 - ₹12,000 = ₹0 (break-even, down from ₹4,000 profit). A wrong answer (e.g., still showing profit) reveals inability to combine simultaneous cost-push and price-deflation shocks — the dual squeeze reform critics highlight.

questions.q: Compare the growth rates of agriculture, industry, and services during 2007-12 from Table 3.1. What does this pattern imply about the structural transformation of the Indian economy?
questions.a: 2007-12: Agriculture 3.2%, Industry 7.4%, Services 10%. Services grew fastest, agriculture slowest. This implies a "service-led" growth model bypassing the traditional agriculture→industry→services transition. A wrong answer stating "industry grew fastest" or "balanced growth" shows failure to read the table correctly and misses the policy critique: reforms failed to create manufacturing jobs that could absorb surplus agricultural labour.

questions.q: Evaluate the argument: "Export-oriented agriculture policy (shifting from food grains to cash crops) benefits farmers by fetching higher international prices."
questions.a: This argument is flawed for three reasons: (1) Small farmers lack storage and market access to benefit from export markets; (2) Food grain diversion raises domestic prices, hurting net food buyers (mostly rural poor); (3) Cash crops (cotton, groundnut) face volatile global prices and pest risks — as seen in Anantapur's crop disease crisis. A student agreeing without qualification misses the food security and risk dimensions central to the NCERT critique.

questions.q: Design a two-pronged policy package to simultaneously address agricultural distress and employment generation, using only instruments mentioned in the chapter (public investment, MSP, credit, infrastructure, skill development).
questions.a: A strong answer proposes: (1) Restore public investment in irrigation, rural roads, and agricultural research (reversing the post-1991 decline) to raise productivity and lower unit costs; (2) Expand MGNREGA-type works to build on-farm infrastructure (water harvesting, land levelling) creating rural employment while improving agricultural capacity. Weak answers suggest only "increase MSP" (fiscal burden, doesn't raise productivity) or "more FDI in retail" (not in chapter, doesn't guarantee farmer income).
